The Ever-Strengthening Spring and the Secret of the Heart: The Torah Teaching, Work and Thought of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh
This article surveys the life and teaching of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh, one of the great Tannaim, focusing on his formative image as the ever-strengthening spring, which represents a creative and innovative force in the study of Torah. The text analyzes his moral conception, which sets the good heart as the foundation that moves all the powers of the soul, alongside a description of his mystical peak in engaging with the Account of the Chariot (Maaseh Merkavah), which unites the human intellect with the Divine Presence. Alongside his praises, the article describes the tragedy of Emmaus, in which Rabbi Elazar's social isolation led to the forgetting of his learning, and thus serves as a reminder of the importance of a community of learners for the preservation of wisdom. The aim of the work is to present a figure who combines halakhic depth, holistic morality and enormous spiritual potential, leaving an eternal mark on the ideal of the Jewish learner.
The Ever-Strengthening Spring and the Secret of the Heart: The Torah Teaching, Work and Thought of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh
The Historical and Spiritual Fabric of the Generation of the Destruction
The figure of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh stands as one of the most fascinating, profound and tragic spiritual phenomena in the historiography of the Tannaitic period. He was active in the second generation, a period in which the Jewish center of gravity shifted from an existence of Temple and sacrifices to an existence of Oral Torah and study in the study hall.[1] As the chosen disciple of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, Rabbi Elazar was not merely a "Torah scholar" in the standard sense of the term, but a creative spiritual force that changed the face of the moral and mystical thought of his time.[1, 2] Analysis of his work requires an understanding of the constant tension between preserving the tradition and renewing it, a tension embodied in his famous image as the "ever-strengthening spring."[3, 4]
To understand the strength of his influence, one must examine the social background from which he emerged. Rabbi Elazar was part of a small, high-quality group of five disciples who surrounded Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai in Jerusalem and afterward in Yavneh.[1, 2] This group served as a spiritual laboratory in which the foundations of rabbinic Judaism were shaped. Within this group, Rabbi Elazar was identified as one capable of outweighing them all—not only in his erudition, but in the intellectual and spiritual quality of his teaching.[1, 4]
The Five Disciples: A Spectrum of Perfections
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, with his deep pedagogical vision, defined for each of his disciples his essential uniqueness. These definitions are not merely praises, but characterizations of "types" of Torah learners, representing different paths in the service of God and in study.
The central tension in the study hall existed between Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus and Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh. Whereas Rabbi Eliezer represented the "plastered cistern"—the archetype of the preserver—Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh represented the "ever-strengthening spring"—the archetype of the creator.[3, 6] Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's decision that Elazar ben Arakh outweighs them all, including Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, testifies to an essential preference for the renewing and creative force over the preserving force, precisely in an era of destruction in which the rebuilding of spiritual worlds was required.[1, 4]
The Phenomenology of the "Ever-Strengthening Spring"
The image of the "ever-strengthening spring" (and sometimes "a flowing stream" in Avot de-Rabbi Natan) is not merely a description of a good memory, but a definition of a religious epistemology.[4] Unlike a cistern, whose water is water that "came to it from outside"—that is, knowledge learned from a teacher that must be preserved as it is—a spring produces water from within itself.[3, 6] The water of a spring wells up from the depths, seeps through the layers of earth and rises to the surface fresh, alive and new at every moment.
The Renewing Intellect and the Inner Wellspring
According to the Maharal of Prague, Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh was endowed with a "root of intellect" and a "strong intellect."[7] The meaning is that his knowledge was not placed in him as an external layer, but became an inseparable part of his essence. When a person learns Torah at such a level, the Torah becomes an inner source of energy. The more he draws from it, the more it strengthens and wells up with greater force.[4] This is a Torah that does not merely repeat the words of the earlier authorities, but derives one thing from another and develops new branches on the trunk of the tradition.
The image of the "flowing stream" adds a layer of momentum. A flowing stream is a force that cannot be stopped; it breaks through boundaries, reshapes its banks and influences all the surroundings through which it passes.[4] Rabbi Elazar's teaching was like this—it did not remain within the walls of the study hall but "let your wellsprings flow outward," radiating over all areas of life, from halakha to mysticism, from morality to leadership.[4]
Implications for the Method of Study
The difference between the "plastered cistern" and the "ever-strengthening spring" reflects two basic pedagogical approaches:
The preservation approach: Focus on precision, on faithful transmission of the "tradition," and on preventing forgetting. The aim is to hand the deposit to the next generation intact.[3, 6]
The development approach: Focus on deep understanding, on connecting different fields, and on developing new ideas. The aim is to turn the learner himself into a source of Torah.[3, 4, 6]
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai recognized the need for both types, but ruled that the quality of the spring is the "decisive" one.[1, 4] Perhaps the reason lies in the fact that in a broken world after a destruction, the natural tendency is to shut oneself in and preserve (a cistern), but the real need is for a force capable of breathing new life and building additional stories (a spring).[6, 7]
The Teaching of the Heart: The Moral Anthropology of Rabbi Elazar
At the center of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh's moral teaching stands the revolutionary determination that a "good heart" is the straight path to which a person should cling.[1, 4, 8] When Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asked his disciples to define the best path, the disciples proposed specific virtues:
Rabbi Eliezer: a good eye (contentment with little and absence of envy).[8]
Rabbi Yehoshua: a good friend (constructive social ties).[8]
Rabbi Yose: a good neighbor (a positive presence in the immediate space).[8]
Rabbi Shimon: one who foresees the outcome (prudent planning and responsibility for the future).[8]
Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh proposed the "good heart," and his teacher decided: "I prefer the words of Elazar ben Arakh to your words, for your words are included in his words."[5, 8, 9]
The Heart as the Source of the Powers
The profound insight of Rabbi Elazar, as the commentators explain (Rabbi Ovadia of Bartenura and the Maharal), is that the heart is not merely a physical organ or a passing emotion, but it is "the mover of all the other powers."[5, 8, 9] The heart is the source from which all actions flow. Even if actions have special organs (the eye sees, the feet walk), the power that arouses and directs is in the heart.[7, 8, 9]
From here derives the all-inclusiveness of the "good heart":
The source of a good eye: One whose heart is good does not envy his fellow and rejoices in his success, because his heart is full of good and has no lack that gives birth to an evil eye.[8]
The foundation for friendship and neighborliness: A good heart is what enables a person to be attentive to others, to rebuke gently and to be present for the other by day and by night.[8]
A compass for foreseeing the outcome: A good heart directs the intellect to see the truth without the distortions of urges and fears, and thereby enables a person to calculate the loss of a commandment against its reward.[8]
The Heart Toward Heaven and Toward People
In Avot de-Rabbi Natan it is stressed that Rabbi Elazar meant "a good heart toward Heaven and a good heart toward fellow creatures."[4, 8] This is a moral unity that does not separate the religious relationship to the Holy One, blessed be He, from the human relationship. A good heart is a state of consciousness of wholeness (integrity) in which a person directs his entire being toward the absolute good. A good heart protects a person from anger, worry and envy—which, according to Rabbi Ovadia of Bartenura, are the main causes of "weakening the power of memory."[8] From here there is a direct connection between a good heart and being a "plastered cistern" or an "ever-strengthening spring"—the inner calm arising from a good heart is the necessary condition for the preservation and development of Torah.[8]
Source: [4, 7, 8]
The Account of the Chariot: The Mystical Peak of Rabbi Elazar
Beyond the teaching of character traits, Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh is considered one of the pioneers of Jewish esoteric teaching—the "Account of the Chariot" (Maaseh Merkavah).[5, 9] The Mishnah in tractate Chagigah sets strict limitations on the study of the secrets of the Chariot, out of fear of mental disturbance or improper use of supernal knowledge. The central condition is that the learner be "wise and understand on his own."[2, 5, 9] The story of Rabbi Elazar's discourse on the road illustrates why he is considered a model of this condition.
The Drama on the Road to Jerusalem
The story described in the Babylonian Talmud (Chagigah 14b) and in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chagigah 2a) places Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh in an open space, far from the protected walls of the study hall.[5, 9] Rabban Yochanan rides on his donkey, a symbol of physical existence, while Rabbi Elazar "drives it behind him"—serving him and seeking to learn. When Rabbi Elazar asks to learn a chapter in the Account of the Chariot, his teacher refuses at first in accordance with the halakhic restrictions.[5, 9]
The turning point occurs when Rabbi Elazar proposes: "Permit me to say before you one thing that you taught me."[5, 9] This proposal reflects the essence of the spring: he does not seek to receive new knowledge passively, but to show how he "understands on his own" what has already been sown within him.[2, 5] The moment Rabban Yochanan hears this, he gets down from the donkey, wraps himself in a prayer shawl and sits on a stone under an olive tree. The physical act of dismounting from the donkey symbolizes the transition from the material world to the world of the secret, and the recognition that Rabbi Elazar is not merely a student, but one from whose throat the Divine Presence speaks.[5, 9]
The Fire, the Angels and the Song of the Trees
The description of the phenomena that accompanied Rabbi Elazar's discourse is among the most impressive in the literature of the Sages:
The descent of fire: Fire came down from heaven and surrounded all the trees in the field.[5, 9] The fire symbolizes the transformation of human speech into a living divine force.
The accompaniment of the ministering angels: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai testifies that the ministering angels accompany them, evidence that Rabbi Elazar's discourse went beyond the boundaries of the human intellect and reached supernal halls.[5, 9]
The song of the trees: The trees opened and said song (Psalms 148: "Praise the Lord from the earth... fruit trees and all cedars").[2, 9] This is a cosmic expression of the fact that Rabbi Elazar's esoteric teaching unites nature with metaphysics.
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, moved by the occasion, kissed Rabbi Elazar on his head and said: "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who gave our father Abraham a son who knows how to understand, to investigate and to expound on the Account of the Chariot."[1, 2] He defined him as one who "expounds well and fulfills well"—that is, a person whose most abstract teaching is expressed in the wholeness of his personality and deeds.[10]
His Halakhic Contribution: Between Asmachta and Tradition
Although Rabbi Elazar's main fame is in the fields of aggadah, morality and the esoteric, there is significant evidence of his activity as a halakhic authority involved in the core issues of the world of Torah law. His halakhic contribution is characterized by the use of Scripture as a living source for halakhic creation.[1]
Handwashing and Purity of the Body
In tractate Chullin (106a) the homily of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh is brought concerning the law of washing the hands.[1] He based the commandment of washing the hands on the verse in Leviticus (15:11): "And anyone whom the one with the discharge touches without having rinsed his hands in water."[1] This homily is a classic example of an "asmachta"—finding an allusion in Scripture for an enactment of the Sages. Rabbi Elazar sought to connect the world of purity and everyday commandments to the root of Scripture, and thereby to give them deeper validity and meaning.[1]
Additional Halakhot in the Jerusalem Talmud
The Jerusalem Talmud preserves additional remnants of his halakhic activity, which attest to his involvement in diverse subjects:
The laws of medumma (tractate Demai): This passage deals with a mixture of terumah (forbidden to non-priests) in ordinary produce. Rabbi Elazar discusses the proportions and rules that permit or forbid eating the mixture, a subject demanding great precision and understanding of the system of the sanctity of foods in the Land of Israel.[1]
The laws of maamar (tractate Yevamot): "Maamar" is a betrothal that a yavam performs with his yevamah before the levirate marriage itself. Rabbi Elazar discusses the question whether this is a complete or partial acquisition, a passage that is at the very heart of the world of marital law and acquisitions. His position testifies to a legal conception that sees in acts between one person and another acquisitions that have both spiritual and practical validity.[1]
The fact that these halakhot survived teaches that in the period of his flourishing, Rabbi Elazar was a senior partner in shaping halakha in his generation. However, the small number of halakhot attributed to him in the later Talmudic discourse attests to the tragedy that befell him later in his life—the loss of his influence and the forgetting of his teaching.[1]
The Tragedy of Emmaus: Forgetting, Isolation and Restoration
The most shaking chapter in the life of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh is his withdrawal from the center of Torah at Yavneh and his move to the town of Emmaus (called in the sources also Dimsit or Diomset).[2, 9] This event became an educational and moral warning for the generations, illustrating the danger of spiritual isolation and of the attraction to the pleasures of this world.
The Reasons for the Move and the Spring's Mistake
After the death of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, the disciples split. While his four colleagues went to Yavneh—where the collective center of the sages of Israel was established—Rabbi Elazar chose to go to Emmaus.[1, 2, 9] The reasons for this were a combination of physical comfort and excessive self-confidence:
His wife's advice and the pleasures of the place: Emmaus was known for "fine waters and a pleasant dwelling."[1, 2] It was a place of healing and delights ("the wine of Pruggita and the waters of Diomset").[2]
The assumption of the "spring": Rabbi Elazar thought that since he was the decisive sage and the "ever-strengthening spring," his colleagues would come to him to learn. He saw himself as a focal point whom everyone needed.[1, 2, 9]
But reality slapped him in the face. His colleagues stayed in Yavneh, a place where "many Torah scholars love the Torah."[5, 9] Rabbi Elazar was left alone. Without the fruitful interaction with colleagues and a teacher, the spring began to dry up. The Gemara in tractate Shabbat describes this in extreme terms: "His learning was uprooted"—his Torah was uprooted from him.[2]
"Their Heart Was Deaf": The Metaphor of Forgetting
The moment at which the force of the disaster was understood was when Rabbi Elazar returned to visit the study hall. He rose to read from the Torah the foundational verse: "This month shall be for you the head of months" (Exodus 12:2). Because of the forgetting, he mistakenly read: "Their heart was deaf" (ha-cheresh hayah libam).[2]
This mistake is not accidental and it carries deep symbolic meaning. Rabbi Elazar, who was the symbol of the "good heart" that understands everything, became one whose heart was sealed and silenced ("the deaf one").[2, 8] The spring that once illuminated the eyes of the sages was unable to read even a simple verse. This is an expression of the fact that Torah is not a static personal possession, but a living flow that needs a community in order to exist.
The story ends in grace: his colleagues the sages had compassion on him and prayed for him, and his Torah returned to him.[2] However, the historical damage was irreversible. His name did not grow great in wisdom as might have been expected from the beginning of his path, and he remained a figure representing the great missed opportunity of his generation.[1]
His Mysterious Identity as Rabbi Nehorai
Another fascinating question in the study of his figure is his identification with Rabbi Nehorai.[5, 11, 12] The Gemara determines in several places (Shabbat 147b, Eruvin 13b): "His name was not Rabbi Nehorai but Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh. Why was he called Rabbi Nehorai? Because he enlightens the eyes of the sages in halakha."[11, 12]
Nehorai: The Light Beyond Forgetting
The name "Nehorai" (light) reflects the deep essence of Rabbi Elazar as perceived by his colleagues. Even after the crisis in Emmaus, he was considered one who knows how to illuminate (lehanhir) halakha—that is, to give it an explanation that penetrates beyond words and illuminates the root of the law.[11, 12] It is possible that the epithet Nehorai was given to him precisely after his Torah returned to him, as testimony that his inner light was not entirely extinguished.
This identification raises the possibility that many of the sayings that appear in the name of "Rabbi Nehorai" actually belong to Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh. One of the most famous of them is: "Go into exile to a place of Torah, and do not say that it will come after you... and do not rely on your own understanding."[5, 12] This saying sounds like a personal confession and a bitter conclusion from his own experience in Emmaus. He warns others not to repeat his mistake—to think that his personal understanding would suffice for him without the company of the sages.[12]
Source: [5, 11, 12]
Connections with Other Sages and the Chain of Transmission
Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh was a central junction in the transmission of esoteric traditions and leadership between key figures in his generation and in the generations before.
Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKaneh and Sefer Tagin
According to the introduction to "Sefer Tagin," Rabbi Elazar was a disciple of Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKaneh.[1, 13] Rabbi Nechunya was a well-known mystical figure (to whom works such as "Sefer HaBahir" and "Ana BeKoach" are attributed).[13] He transmitted to Rabbi Elazar the chain of tradition concerning the writing of STaM (Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot) with the special crowns and tagin on the letters.[1] This tradition was passed from Rabbi Elazar to his colleague Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah and from there to Rabbi Akiva.[1]
The connection between the two deepens the understanding of Rabbi Elazar as a link in a chain of sages who engaged in the combination of halakhic practice (the writing of STaM) and the mystical secret embedded in the shape of the letters.[1, 13] The fact that both of them lived in Emmaus at some stage hints at a spiritual community that existed there around these esoteric studies.[1]
The Successful Adviser
In Midrash Tehillim, Rabbi Elazar is described as one whom "everyone needs for his counsel."[1, 14] He developed a theory of counsel as a kind of prophecy: "Every counsel that is for the sake of Heaven will in the end be fulfilled."[1, 14] This conception connects again to his teaching of the heart—successful counsel does not derive only from logical analysis but from purity of heart and intention. He served as an adviser and comforter, and many saw in him a figure whose words were fulfilled in a wondrous manner.[14]
Death, Burial and Legacy
The end of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh's days is shrouded in mystery. The traditions about his burial place are varied and reflect the admiration felt for him throughout the generations:
Alma: an identification from the twelfth century.[1]
Dalton: an identification from the eleventh century.[1]
Safed and Tiberias: later identifications.[1]
His legacy remained engraved in the history of the people of Israel not because of the quantity of mishnayot he wrote (which is surprisingly small), but because of the quality and the direction he set. He left behind the figure of the "spring" as an ideal for every Torah learner—the aspiration to turn study into a living, welling, ever-strengthening force.[3, 4, 6]
Summary of the Findings and Insights
Examination of the figure of Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh yields a picture of a spiritual giant who embodied the transition from linear wisdom to holistic wisdom. The three central points in his teaching are the pillars of his Torah:
The spring: The ability to renew from an inner wellspring and to understand one thing from another.[4]
The heart: The recognition of the heart as the moral and cognitive center that contains within it all the other character traits.[8]
The secret: The ability to translate abstract study into a living spiritual experience of fire and angels.[5]
The tragedy of his forgetting serves as an eternal reminder that even the "spring" needs the channel of a community and a spiritual center in order to continue to flow. Nevertheless, the very existence of Rabbi Elazar in the study hall of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai laid the foundations for a Judaism that combines mystical depth with moral responsibility and halakhic precision, a Judaism that "expounds well and fulfills well."[1, 7, 10]
